evidence_effectiveness: A shared logging microservice capturing timestamps, I/O metadata, model version and rationale with chain-of-custody would meet Article 12(1) and (2) traceability requirements.

evidence_originality: Instrumenting model-serving pipelines with middleware to emit structured compliance events for mandated log fields is common, mundane logging engineering practice.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces new pipeline tools and capture processes but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: The proposal implements the mandatory Article 12(3) logging requirements for Annex III biometric systems using standard middleware, which violates no legal, social or political norms.

evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab will meet the Article 12 record-keeping mandate and keep biometric R&D on schedule, which is the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Emitting a structured compliance event at the decision boundary that records start/end times, reference database version, matched input data and verifier identities would meet Article 12(3) logging requirements for Annex III point 1(a) systems.

evidence_originality: Treating Article 12 log fields as observable experimental variables and mapping ablations onto the schema is unusual and shows imagination relative to typical lab responses.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal weaves mandated logging into the scientific workflow, changing how R&D relates to compliance rather than treating compliance as an afterthought.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing a peer-reviewable methodology for regulatory compliance is socially and legally unobjectionable and aligns with norms of reproducible research.
evidence_implementability: Drafting an internal protocol and a journal submission is a reasonably feasible methodological effort for a methods group without major engineering overhaul.
evidence_applicability: The framework directly targets how the lab can meet Article 12 logging mandates by embedding required log fields into experimental design from day one.
evidence_effectiveness: It would make compliance records serve as experimental evidence, contributing to traceability but it does not itself build the automatic logging infrastructure mandated by Article 12.

evidence_originality: Automated log-completeness gates in CI/CD are a common DevOps compliance practice and the proposal describes standard shift-left testing with no novel mechanism.

evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance checks in QA is a socially, legally and politically normal engineering practice with no normative conflict.
evidence_implementability: Adding scripted log-field verification to CI/CD requires modest pipeline changes and test data but is reasonably feasible for an R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the mandate to ensure Article 12 event types are captured before deployment.
evidence_effectiveness: It will catch missing log fields early and reduce rework, contributing to but not fully guaranteeing lifetime traceability and post-market monitoring required by the Act.

evidence_originality: The centralized living documentation platform with stewards and quarterly audits is a standard compliance operations practice commonly described for regulated AI.

evidence_acceptability: Maintaining up-to-date technical files and audits is socially, legally and politically expected for high-risk AI.
evidence_implementability: Standing up a platform and assigning stewards requires organizational changes but is reasonably feasible for an R&D lab.

evidence_originality: Defining formal semantics for event-relevance in AI logs is rare and imaginative, moving beyond standard logging checklists toward a novel theoretical contribution.

evidence_acceptability: A formal research programme to clarify logging relevance violates no legal, social or political norms and is an unobjectionable academic activity.

evidence_applicability: It directly targets Article 12(2)’s requirement to record events relevant for risk, traceability and monitoring of high-risk AI systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It would improve selection of what to log under Article 12(2) but does not itself build the required automatic logging infrastructure to meet the mandate.

evidence_originality: Reusing existing model-monitoring infrastructure for regulatory logging is a common cost-saving compliance tactic expected from AI R&D labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It integrates compliance logging into ongoing R&D monitoring, changing how R&D and compliance obligations relate while still treating compliance as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Reusing internal model-monitoring and data-pipeline infrastructure for mandated logging aligns with legal requirements and does not offend norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing metrics dashboard with event-log storage, retention scheduling and query interfaces is reasonably feasible using the already funded data-ops team.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly builds the automatic event logging and post-market monitoring backend required by Article 12 and Article 72 for high-risk AI systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the shared infrastructure would provide lifetime logs and traceability needed for conformity assessment, risk identification and post-market monitoring.

evidence_originality: The proposal offers an unusual, research-driven taxonomy for log events rather than a standard engineering implementation.

evidence_acceptability: A methodological study and published taxonomy does not violate legal norms or professional sensibilities.

evidence_effectiveness: A reference specification would guide logging design and contribute to compliance, though it does not itself deploy the mandated logging system.

evidence_originality: Stress-testing log persistence for multi-year regulatory traceability is an interesting but familiar systems evaluation approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds a formal benchmarking process to compliance planning while still treating logging as a downstream operational requirement.
evidence_acceptability: Benchmarking storage performance is a routine engineering practice that raises no legal or social concerns.
evidence_implementability: The experiment uses existing sandbox clusters and synthetic streams to benchmark time-series and object stores, requiring only engineering time rather than production changes.
evidence_applicability: Choosing a viable long-term log store directly addresses the Article 12 requirement to enable automatic recording over system lifetime.
evidence_effectiveness: The benchmark informs architecture choice and avoids late storage failures, but does not itself deploy the mandated logging capability.

evidence_originality: Combining tiered open-science releases with automated documentation versioning for EU AI Act compliance is unusual among typical logging-focused responses expected from labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Tiered release policy and an automated documentation generator embed compliance documentation into the research sharing workflow, changing how R&D and compliance interrelate.
evidence_acceptability: The tiered release approach respects Recital 71 transparency goals while avoiding unsafe disclosure, making it socially and legally acceptable though less common than closed compliance.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a tiered policy and building an automated documentation generator with versioning is a reasonably feasible institutional change piloted on two projects this quarter.

evidence_effectiveness: Automated documentation versioning helps maintain Recital 71 compliance but does not itself implement the mandated automatic event logging required by Article 12(1)-(3).

evidence_originality: Applying a CI/CD modification gate specifically to EU AI Act substantial-modification logging is uncommon in practice and shows imaginative operationalization of legal text.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It embeds compliance checking into the R&D build pipeline rather than treating logging as a post-hoc administrative task.
evidence_acceptability: Blocking deployment pending engineer sign-off for compliance is standard engineering governance and does not offend legal or workplace sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: It reuses the existing CI runner and adds configurable rules and a sign-off step, which is feasible but requires defining modification thresholds and workflow changes.
evidence_applicability: The gate directly addresses compliance with Article 12's logging and modification traceability during R&D builds.
evidence_effectiveness: It targets the traceability requirement for substantial modifications under Article 12(2)(a) by auto-flagging changes that need new logging baselines.

evidence_originality: The versioned living-documentation repository with a steward and automated change alerts is a familiar software-governance practice applied to AI compliance rather than an ingenious or surprising invention.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new documentation tools and processes but keeps compliance as a separate documentation exercise and does not change the relationship between R&D and the logging mandate.
evidence_acceptability: Maintaining up-to-date technical documentation and regular internal audits are standard, legally encouraged compliance practices that raise no social or legal concerns.
evidence_implementability: Building a versioned repository, assigning stewards, and automating change-trigger alerts is feasible with existing tools and requires only moderate organizational change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets technical documentation upkeep under Recital 71 rather than the automatic event-logging requirements of Article 12 that define the stated problem.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if implemented perfectly, a living documentation system does not create the automatic logs required by Article 12(1)-(3), so it will not meet the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Building an open-source reference implementation specifically for Article 12 Annex III schemas is unusual for an R&D lab and shows imagination in turning a mandate into public contribution.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces a reusable open-source logging library and standards engagement that reframes compliance from per-project overhead to a shared asset and market position.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an EU-friendly open-source compliance tool and engaging with CEN-CENELEC forums aligns with norms and strengthens public-sector credibility.

evidence_applicability: It directly targets the Article 12 mandate to technically allow automatic event logging and reduce compliance engineering per high-risk project.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the library would provide the required logging schemas and traceability capabilities for Annex III systems, solving the core logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Converting a compliance logging obligation into a customer-facing sales asset via a living traceability white paper is unusual and shows imagination beyond standard internal documentation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The idea changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by weaving logging transparency into marketing and offerings, making compliance a market differentiator.
evidence_acceptability: Proactive transparency about traceability is socially, legally and commercially acceptable and aligns with common industry communications norms.
evidence_implementability: Producing a quarterly co-authored web-hosted document and adding it to contract packages is a low-cost, non-radical process change for an R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses adaptation to the Article 12 mandate by communicating logging practices rather than implementing the required automatic recording capability.
evidence_effectiveness: A public white paper does not create the technical logging capabilities, event recording, or retention required by Article 12 and Recital 71, so it will not solve the mandate.

evidence_originality: Authoring and publishing a community benchmark with reference implementations and a position paper to conformity-assessment bodies is unusual and shows imagination beyond routine internal logging work.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces an open, peer-reviewed traceability schema and reframes the lab’s relationship to compliance by positioning traceability as a research methodology and the lab as a knowledge-setter for the scientific community.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing an open traceability framework and engaging conformity-assessment bodies is a common, norm-conforming scientific contribution that violates no legal or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A three-researcher working group can draft, validate against existing prototypes and release GitHub reference implementations with a position paper within reasonable researcher time and cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal drafts a minimum metadata schema for timestamps, data lineage, model versioning and human-in-the-loop identifiers and validates it against the lab’s own Annex III 1(a) biometric-ID prototypes to satisfy Article 12 logging.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if the schema were adopted, the lab would still need to implement automatic event logging in its high-risk systems, so the standard contributes to but does not by itself fully solve the mandated traceability requirement.

evidence_originality: Treating logs as the native experimental record and repurposing them for a longitudinal failure-mode dataset is unusual and shows some imagination beyond a simple compliance add-on.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It embeds compliance logging into the experimental workflow and treats traceability as the default research record, changing the relationship between the lab’s R&D and its compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Automatic timestamped logging for traceability aligns with the AI Act requirements and with scientific record-keeping norms and offends no legal or social sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Wrapping existing MLflow / Hugging Face orchestration with structured event schemas and mandating use in the next quarter requires a pipeline refactor but builds on familiar tools, making it reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly emits timestamped event logs of inputs, reference databases and human verification steps mapped to Article 12(2)(a)-(c) and the four Annex III minimums for high-risk AI systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If done, the logging-native infrastructure would automatically record the mandated events over the system lifetime and eliminate costly retro-fit engineering, solving the stated logging mandate.

evidence_originality: A public benchmark for detecting Article 79(1) risk events from lifetime logs is unusual and shows imagination in turning regulatory data into a community research problem.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal reframes mandatory logging from a compliance cost into a shared scientific research programme that changes how R&D and compliance obligations relate and advances interpretability science.
evidence_acceptability: Publicly releasing even anonymised deployment traces and inviting external analysis is somewhat uncommon but does not inherently offend legal or social sensibilities when done with regulator co-design.
evidence_implementability: Creating an anonymised public log release, hosting an annual open-source evaluation and co-developing scoring rubrics with regulators requires significant data-privacy review, infrastructure and sustained partnership effort beyond routine logging.
evidence_applicability: The benchmark directly addresses the implied need to know what logging can and cannot reveal about risk-relevant events under Article 12 and Article 79(1).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would improve collective understanding of log-based risk detection and thus contribute to meeting the traceability and monitoring aims of the mandate, but it does not itself install the required logging capabilities.

evidence_originality: Forward-compatible logging schemas with object-store retention is a common, mundane engineering solution routinely expected in regulated systems.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tools and processes for logging but still treats compliance as improved logging practice rather than changing the lab’s R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Using versioned schemas and S3-compatible lifecycle rules is conventional data-engineering compliance practice that violates no legal, social or political norms.
evidence_implementability: Implementing it requires a data-engineering team to define schemas, build immutable storage with hot/cold tiers and write migration tooling, which is reasonably feasible but more than a non-radical change.
evidence_applicability: The proposal designs a lifetime event schema and retention architecture to meet Article 12’s automatic logging, traceability and post-market monitoring mandate for high-risk AI systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Versioned JSON schemas with semantic tags plus immutable tiered object storage with migration tooling would enable continuous, queryable logs through model updates and substantial modifications as required by Article 12(2)(a).

evidence_originality: Embedding audit logging natively into model execution graphs with compiled logging interfaces is unusual and shows imagination beyond bolt-on instrumentation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The program weaves event-logging semantics into training pipelines and inference graphs and reframes compliance as architectural research, changing how R&D relates to logging obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Building auditable, log-native models for EU AI Act compliance is an uncommon technical strategy that does not offend legal or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Prototyping three reference architectures with compiled logging interfaces and measuring overhead against baselines requires significant engineering change and research cost.
evidence_applicability: Capturing audit-relevant events natively in training and inference directly addresses the Article 12 mandate to technically allow automatic recording of logs over the system lifetime.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, native logging would provide the required automatic, traceable event recording for high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime.

evidence_originality: Living documentation with version-control lockstep updates and a release gate is a common, mundane compliance measure in regulated software development.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces tools and process steps for documentation but still treats compliance as standard technical-file maintenance without changing the relationship between R&D and logging obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Assigning a technical writer per product line and adding a documentation-currency release gate is a common compliance practice that violates no legal, social or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Implementing a writer role and a documentation gate requires some organizational changes but is reasonably feasible within an R&D lab’s existing version-control and release workflow.
evidence_applicability: The proposal creates a living technical file and release gate, which addresses Recital 71 documentation duties related to traceability rather than the automatic event logging capabilities mandated by Article 12.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic logs for use periods, reference databases, matching inputs and verifier identity required by Article 12(1)-(3) are not produced by updating technical documentation, so the logging mandate remains unsolved.

evidence_originality: Dedicated audit pipelines for mandated biometric logging fields are common compliance responses expected from regulated labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a dedicated pipeline and tamper-evident sealing for logs but still treats compliance as logging practice rather than changing the lab's R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Partnering legal-compliance to define retention and access controls and using tamper-evident hashes for mandated biometric logs conforms to EU AI Act norms and does not offend sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending existing database-provenance tooling with tagging and sealing requires infrastructure engineering changes but builds on current systems, making it reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly implements Article 12(1)-(3) minimum logging fields for Annex III 1(a) biometric systems, which is the stated compliance problem.
evidence_effectiveness: The pipeline will satisfy traceability and post-market monitoring requirements for the most sensitive biometric systems, though it does not address logging for other high-risk AI systems in the lab.

evidence_originality: Tying documentation currency to stage-gate reviews and assigning it to PI lab managers is an interesting process integration but is a familiar project-governance practice in regulated R&D.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal weaves technical-documentation updates into existing research milestone stage-gates, making compliance a recurring part of the R&D workflow rather than a separate launch dossier.
evidence_acceptability: Using existing grant progress meetings and lab-manager ownership is a common, non-norm-violating compliance approach.
evidence_implementability: The change reuses meeting structures already funded and adds only a checklist gate, so it is easy to implement at low cost.
evidence_applicability: The idea directly addresses the need to keep records and technical documentation current throughout the system lifetime as required by Recital 71 for high-risk AI systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A milestone-gated documentation checklist will help maintain up-to-date records and continuity across staff rotation, but it does not by itself provide the automatic event logging mandated by Article 12(1)-(2).

evidence_originality: Framing mandated operational logs as a new scientific data category with standardized anonymization and cross-institutional sharing is unusual and shows imagination beyond routine compliance documentation.

evidence_acceptability: Releasing a de-identified sample corpus under a data-use agreement with anonymization schemas is an uncommon strategy but does not violate legal norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Drafting a whitepaper, building a pilot anonymization pipeline for one system class and negotiating agreements with three universities requires some changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The idea addresses the implied problem of how to adapt R&D in response to mandated logging, rather than directly solving the identified logging implementation requirement.
evidence_effectiveness: Creating a compliance-telemetry research framework contributes to adapting R&D around the logging mandate but does not by itself ensure the automatic logging and traceability required by Article 12.

evidence_originality: Wrapping biometric matchers with a sidecar audit middleware is an interesting engineering pattern but is a familiar observability approach rather than rare or ingenious.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces a new instrumentation tool and process for logging but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing the lab’s R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: An append-only tamper-evident logging sidecar that records mandated audit data is a common, norm-compliant compliance practice.

evidence_applicability: The middleware is designed specifically to provide the automatic event logging traceability required by Article 12 and Recital 71 for high-risk AI systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It automatically captures reference database version, input pointers, match results and verifier identity as required by Article 12(3), so if implemented it would meet the logging mandate for Annex III 1(a) systems.

evidence_originality: Automatically emitting compliance-aligned logs from the experiment runner is an interesting but familiar MLOps practice rather than an ingenious or surprising invention.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Logging is woven into the scientific workflow so research velocity is preserved while outputs become compliance-ready, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance logging into experiment pipelines is a common, norm-conforming strategy that does not violate legal, social or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Redesigning the internal experiment runner and adding a mandatory telemetry layer to an MLflow-based harness is reasonably feasible for an R&D lab with existing MLOps infrastructure.

evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, native emission of model version, data provenance, hyperparameters and outputs with validation against Article 12(3) fields would make lab results immediately compliance-ready for handoff.

evidence_originality: Turning a regulatory logging obligation into an open-source product with usage analytics is unusual for an R&D lab and shows imaginative commercial reuse of compliance work.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: By creating a distributable compliance SDK, the lab changes its relationship to regulation from cost centre to market offering, stretching the paradigm beyond standard logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Open-sourcing a compliance middleware under a permissive licence aligns with industry norms and does not violate legal or sensibility norms.

evidence_effectiveness: The SDK provides reusable logging schemas that directly enable automatic event recording and traceability required by Article 12, so internal systems can meet the mandate without custom engineering per model.

evidence_originality: Packaging regulatory logging as a client-facing assurance feature is unusual and shows imagination for an R&D lab response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the relationship between R&D and compliance by creating a new client-facing offering born from the mandate, stretching the paradigm beyond standard logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: A contractual, read-only log-exposure dossier and assurance brief is a common client assurance practice that violates no legal or sensibility norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a gated read-only log-exposure endpoint plus co-authored one-page briefs requires modest engineering and marketing work and is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It solves an implied commercial adaptation problem of client assurance and competitive differentiation that is related to, but not the direct technical logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The proposal markets and exposes logging architecture to clients rather than building the automatic event recording and Article 12(1)-(3) fields required for high-risk systems.

evidence_originality: Treating mandatory lifetime event logs as a primary empirical dataset for post-deployment interpretability is rare and shows imaginative repurposing of compliance data.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The programme makes compliance logs a source of frontier science, changing the relationship between the lab’s R&D and its compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Using anonymised production logs for internal reliability research is an unusual but legally permissible and professionally unobjectionable strategy under the AI Act.
evidence_implementability: Assembling an anonymised cross-project log corpus and developing statistical/causal drift methods requires new staff and data infrastructure but builds on logs the regulation already mandates to be collected.
evidence_applicability: It clearly applies to the adaptation side of the stated problem by reusing Article 12 logs for research rather than merely logging for compliance.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would create scientific value from the mandated data stream and incentivise good logging, but it does not by itself guarantee that the logging mandate is met.

evidence_originality: Information-theoretic bounds on minimal sufficient logs for traceability is unusual and shows imagination beyond standard compliance tooling.

evidence_acceptability: Studying minimal sufficient logging for EU AI Act compliance is a common, norm-conforming research response that violates no legal, social or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: The work requires developing causal information-flow metrics and empirical validation on synthetic workloads, which is reasonably feasible for an R&D lab but needs dedicated research effort beyond routine engineering.

evidence_effectiveness: If the bounds could be derived, they would inform compliant system design and avoid maximal data collection, but a theoretical study alone does not install logging capabilities required by Article 12(1)-(3).

evidence_originality: A shared middleware SDK for amortised compliance logging is a common, mundane response that experienced evaluators would expect from AI R&D labs.

evidence_acceptability: Automated capture of the Article 12 logs via standard middleware is a common compliance practice that violates no legal, social or business norms.

evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how the lab must meet the Article 12 automatic logging and traceability requirements for high-risk AI systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the shared layer automatically records start/end timestamps, reference-database identifiers, matched inputs and verifier identities as mandated by Article 12(1)-(3), thereby solving the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Formalising risk-relevant events as a monitoring-signal class with small auxiliary models that emit structured alert logs is unusual and shows imagination for compliance work.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It changes the lab’s relationship to compliance by weaving logging into core R&D as an active trustworthy-AI research programme rather than an administrative add-on.

evidence_implementability: Building and validating real-time in-system anomaly/out-of-distribution detectors, failure-mode benchmark datasets and separate auxiliary log-emitting models requires substantial new research engineering effort beyond standard logging.

evidence_effectiveness: If it could be built, the in-system detectors would automatically flag risk-relevant events and feed the Article 72 post-market-monitoring pipeline, solving the stated logging mandate.

evidence_originality: A compliance-by-default logging middleware for prototypes is a common, mundane industry practice rather than ingenious or surprising.

evidence_acceptability: The SDK enforces the legally required Article 12 logging without collecting extra personal data or violating research norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a thin agent that hooks into existing model-serving and data-ingestion pipelines with a config-driven YAML schema requires platform engineering but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly provides automatic recording of the event classes demanded by Article 12(2)(a)-(c) for high-risk AI prototypes.

evidence_originality: An open benchmark suite that standardises Article 12 log schemas, reference-database checksums and paragraph 3 biometric fields is unusual in AI R&D and shows imagination beyond ad-hoc internal logging scripts.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The toolkit reframes compliance from passive logging burden into shared scientific infrastructure and community leadership, changing the lab’s relationship to its regulatory obligations while still treating compliance as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing permissively licensed compliance tooling via an institutional repository and partnering with universities is a common, norm-aligned academic practice that violates no legal or social sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building and co-maintaining an open-source toolkit with two partner universities and publishing a peer-reviewed schema paper within eighteen months requires dedicated engineering and academic effort but is reasonably feasible for a research lab.

evidence_originality: Reframing compulsory compliance logs as a longitudinal scientific dataset for drift detection is unusual and shows imagination beyond routine logging.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging into core scientific work and creates new research outputs from compliance data, changing how R&D relates to regulatory obligations.
evidence_acceptability: The proposal uses mandated logs for research and open publication, which aligns with regulatory transparency goals and does not violate legal or ethical norms.
evidence_implementability: Building six-month rolling log pipelines and validating detection algorithms requires new engineering and methodology work but is feasible within an R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: The project directly addresses the mandate to technically allow automatic recording of events and to enable traceability and post-market monitoring.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy logging requirements and generate useful monitoring tools, though it does not by itself guarantee full Annex III point-specific record keeping for all high-risk systems.

evidence_originality: Repurposing Article 12 monitoring duties into an eighteen-month methodological research programme with external dissemination is unusual and imaginative for an R&D lab facing compliance.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal reframes compliance logging as a core R&D work-package that produces publishable methods and reference implementations, fundamentally changing how the lab relates research to regulatory obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Allocating internal staff to build monitoring methods that meet EU traceability requirements is socially, legally and politically acceptable and violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: Hiring two senior researchers and one data engineer for eighteen months requires significant staffing and time but is a reasonably feasible internal reallocation.

evidence_effectiveness: While the methods would improve use of logs for post-market monitoring, they do not themselves guarantee the automatic logging capability mandated by Article 12(1), so the problem is only partially solved.

evidence_originality: A compliance stage-gate tied to development sprints is a common, mundane risk-management practice in regulated R&D settings.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The idea introduces new process elements such as per-project reviewers and sprint-boundary sign-offs but still treats compliance as conventional logging practice without changing the lab’s core R&D paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: The proposal is a formal internal compliance review and sign-off for high-risk AI projects, which is a socially, legally and politically conventional governance practice.
evidence_implementability: Assigning a dedicated compliance reviewer per project and inserting a record-keeping review at each sprint boundary requires organizational changes and staffing but is reasonably feasible with existing R&D management structures.

evidence_acceptability: Building internal instrumentation to meet legal record-keeping requirements violates no norms, laws or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Integrating a library into an existing prototyping SDK with configurable retention and schema versioning requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible for an R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: The middleware is designed to auto-capture Article 12(2) event types and Annex III 1(a) minimums for every prototype, directly addressing the lab’s mandate to meet automatic record-keeping.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the shared library would provide lifetime automatic recording of timestamps, reference-database provenance, matched inputs and verifier IDs as required by Article 12, thereby solving the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: The proposal describes standard internal governance documentation that experienced labs routinely produce for regulatory record-keeping.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It treats Article 12 as a documentation task without altering R&D processes or the lab’s research-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Institutional data-governance policies for retention, encryption and role-based access are standard, lawful business practice.
evidence_implementability: Creating an internal policy document requires compliance office drafting and approval with minimal technical changes.
evidence_applicability: Drafting a retention and access policy directly provides the governance needed to meet Article 12 logging and Article 72 post-market monitoring demands.
evidence_effectiveness: A retention policy improves traceability and inspection readiness but does not create the automatic event-logging capability required by Article 12(1).

evidence_originality: Requiring a compliance sign-off document before code freeze is a common, mundane design-gate practice in regulated engineering.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds a new document and review gate but still treats compliance as separate logging practice rather than changing the R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: A mandatory logging specification aligned with the EU AI Act violates no legal or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Issuing a template and adding a design-review sign-off is a low-cost, non-radical process change.
evidence_applicability: Creating a pre-code-freeze Logging Specification directly addresses how the lab meets the Article 12 record-keeping mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The specification ensures logging requirements are mapped to Article 12 before build, which will help meet traceability obligations but does not itself implement automatic logs.

evidence_originality: Reframing benchmark harnesses for continuous drift reporting that doubles as compliance documentation is unusual and imaginative.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal weaves logging data into the scientific evaluation workflow to produce publications, changing how R&D and compliance interact.
evidence_acceptability: Using internal production samples for evaluation and publishing aggregate statistics is a common, norm-compliant research practice.
evidence_implementability: It requires redirecting about ten percent of compute and analyst time to run evaluations on production samples, which is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: It directly targets post-market monitoring and traceability required by Article 12(2)(b) and Article 72 via log-driven drift reports.
evidence_effectiveness: It leverages existing logs to support monitoring but does not itself create the mandatory automatic event logging capability required by Article 12(1).

evidence_originality: Reusable SDKs for mandated logging are a common, mundane engineering compliance pattern.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It centralizes logging into a shared tool yet leaves R&D objectives and the lab’s research direction unchanged, treating compliance as logging practice.
evidence_acceptability: Automatic logging of the mandated event categories aligns with Article 12 legal requirements and does not offend social, legal or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Building a reusable SDK that wraps inference pipelines and enforces metadata tagging requires platform engineering effort and codebase integration but uses standard logging practices.
evidence_applicability: It directly provides automatic recording of Article 12(2) and 12(3) events for all high-risk systems the lab builds.
evidence_effectiveness: With full rollout every high-risk system would automatically log required timestamps, reference databases, input-data matches and verification personnel identifiers.

evidence_originality: Pooling mandated Article 12 logs into a shared, longitudinal research corpus released to the wider community is unusual for compliance work and shows imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a shared longitudinal corpus and reframes mandated logging as the core of the lab’s research program, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: The proposal relies on anonymized sharing under data-protection compliance, which is unusual for operational logs but does not contravene legal or social norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a cross-system ingestion and governance pipeline with anonymization and periodic community release requires significant engineering, legal review and sustained resources.
evidence_applicability: Aggregating lifetime logs with an ingestion and governance pipeline directly addresses how the lab meets Article 12 record-keeping and adapts R&D to the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the corpus pipeline would provide the automatic, lifecycle logging required by Article 12 while turning compliance data into usable post-market monitoring research.

evidence_originality: A two-week infrastructure mapping sprint against regulatory data fields is a common, mundane audit practice in regulated engineering environments.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal is a standard compliance gap analysis that treats Article 12 logging as an existing logging practice to be checked, leaving the lab’s R&D and compliance relationship unchanged.
evidence_acceptability: Mapping existing observability stacks to legal requirements is a conventional, norm-conforming compliance engineering activity.
evidence_implementability: A senior-engineer sprint using ELK, Prometheus and Kafka to produce one-page matrices per system is reasonably feasible with limited time and cost.
evidence_applicability: The audit directly maps deployed high-risk pipelines to Article 12(3)(a)–(d) minimum fields to decide where engineering hours are needed for the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Identifying coverage gaps and certifiable systems informs resource allocation for compliance but does not itself create the required logs or modify R&D.

evidence_originality: Immutable append-only log retention with role-based access for EU AI Act Article 12 compliance is a common, mundane industry approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new elements such as tiered WORM storage and per-field schemas but still treats compliance as logging practice without changing the lab’s R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Building immutable append-only logs with role-based access and lifetime retention to meet Article 12 is a standard legally required compliance practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: A three-month engineering spike to prototype WORM object storage, draft per-field schemas and stress-test audit retrieval is reasonably feasible before an Annex III(a) product ships to an EU customer.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet Article 12 record-keeping and logging requirements for high-risk AI in an R&D lab.
evidence_effectiveness: The tiered architecture captures use timestamps, reference-database pointer, matched input data and verifier identity with immutable lifetime retention, which would solve the logging mandate for biometric high-risk systems.

evidence_originality: Framing EU logging obligations as an epistemology of stochastic system documentation with information-theoretic limits is unusual and imaginative for an R&D lab response.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It recasts compliance from a logging practice into a fundamental research agenda on interpretability, changing the relationship between the lab's R&D and its compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Open academic publication on documentation limits is a normative research activity that violates no laws or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Conducting theoretical papers and case studies with existing prototypes uses existing research capacity and does not require new regulatory approvals or production systems.
evidence_applicability: The research directly engages Recital 71's documentation requirements and aims to inform how tightly internal documentation can and must be written, linking to the lab's need to adapt R&D to the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: The programme produces theoretical and empirical papers on information-theoretic limits of documentation rather than logging infrastructure, so it informs documentation policy but does not deliver the mandatory automatic logs required by Article 12.

evidence_originality: While logging is expected, explicitly designing a forward-compatible schema governance pipeline with backfill tooling is less common and shows imagination beyond basic logging.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds schema tooling and governance around logs without redefining how R&D is conducted or integrating compliance into scientific method.
evidence_acceptability: Versioned schemas and schema registries are standard data-engineering practices with no legal or ethical conflicts.
evidence_implementability: Adopting Avro/Protobuf registry and migration tooling requires engineering effort and process change but is a reasonably feasible measure for an R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets the specific requirement to keep event logs queryable over the system's lifetime as mandated in Article 12(1) and Recital 71.
evidence_effectiveness: It directly addresses lifetime traceability and auditability of logs required by Article 12(1) but does not cover log content selection or post-market monitoring processes.

evidence_originality: A permanent compliance analyst unit with a dashboard and escalation for log surveillance is a common, mundane governance practice in regulated industries.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds an oversight layer while keeping R&D separate from compliance, treating logging as standard administrative practice without changing the lab’s way of working.
evidence_acceptability: A dedicated compliance surveillance cell for high-risk AI logs is socially and legally expected and does not violate norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Setting up a small permanent unit with a monitoring dashboard, weekly exception reports and a 48-hour escalation protocol requires hiring and integration but is reasonably feasible with moderate resources.
evidence_applicability: Continuous review of deployed system logs directly addresses Article 12(2)’s requirements to record events relevant for risk identification, post-market monitoring and operation monitoring.
evidence_effectiveness: The cell improves traceability, post-market monitoring under Articles 72 and 79(1) and operation monitoring, but it does not itself create the mandated automatic event logging capability.

evidence_originality: Building a shared logging library for regulated prototypes is a common, mundane engineering response expected from labs facing Article 12.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The SDK introduces a new logging tool and process but still treats compliance as separate logging practice rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Using a standard middleware to automatically record mandated logs violates no legal, social or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Creating a thin Python/Rust library with pluggable backends and wiring it into the starter template requires some engineering changes but is reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly provides automatic event logging for high-risk prototypes as required by Article 12(1)-(2).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the SDK would give lifetime traceability in every build and meet the mandated logging categories without regard to cost.

evidence_originality: Treating log-informativeness as an architectural metric via systematic ablations is unusual in AI labs and shows imaginative reframing.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance from post-hoc engineering to a first-class scientific axis, changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A transparent research program on compliance-relevant architecture is socially and legally unobjectionable.
evidence_implementability: Running controlled architecture ablations, measuring log-informativeness and publishing results requires dedicated research staff and compute beyond routine compliance engineering.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the lab's need to adapt R&D in response to Article 12 by making traceability a design criterion for model development.
evidence_effectiveness: The program does not deliver immediate logging infrastructure required by Article 12 but it creates architectural knowledge that can improve native log granularity for future high-risk systems.

evidence_originality: Pre-wiring Article 12-specific event schemas into a pluggable emitter for all prototypes is unusual for R&D labs and shows imagination in preventing retrofit costs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Integrating logging schemas into the base prototyping template weaves compliance into the R&D workflow rather than treating it as a post-hoc retrofit.
evidence_acceptability: Mandatory instrumentation for regulatory logging is a standard compliance practice that violates no legal norms or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Extending the internal prototyping framework to include a pluggable event-emitter template requires engineering effort and training but uses existing tooling, making it reasonably feasible.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses the stated problem of meeting the automatic record-keeping mandate by embedding capture in every high-risk AI prototype.
evidence_effectiveness: Providing timestamped events for risk identification, post-market monitoring hooks and operational telemetry directly satisfies Article 12(1)-(2) logging mandates from prototype onward.

evidence_originality: The proposal describes reusing mandated logs as an internal research dataset for reproducibility and failure analysis, an interesting MLOps reuse idea but not ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves compliance logging into the science workflow by standardising schemas and opening anonymised researcher streams, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Standardising logs and providing anonymised read-only access complies with Article 12 and does not violate legal, privacy or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires schema standardisation across all high-risk projects in two sprint cycles and a lightweight dashboard, which is reasonably feasible using already funded logging infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses how the lab meets the Article 12 logging mandate and adapts R&D accordingly.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would satisfy automatic event recording, traceability and post-market monitoring while creating secondary research value and audit defence.

evidence_originality: The proposal describes a standard MLOps data-architecture practice of a unified log schema and versioned storage rather than an ingenious or surprising approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new tools and processes for logging but keeps compliance as separate logging practice without altering the lab's R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Designing a shared data dictionary and using existing object storage violates no legal, social or business norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires a small cross-functional team and prototyping on existing infrastructure, which is reasonably feasible though not trivial.
evidence_applicability: The schema explicitly targets Article 12(1) lifetime logging and Article 72 post-market monitoring for high-risk AI systems.
evidence_effectiveness: A stable long-lived schema with retention and field versioning directly enables automatic lifetime logging and post-market monitoring required by Article 12.

evidence_originality: Inherently log-emitting neural/hybrid layers with temporal context and uncertainty propagation is rare and imaginative relative to expected logging responses from AI R&D labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It re-integrates compliance into core R&D by making logging an inherent property of model architectures rather than a post-hoc add-on and addresses the larger research problem of interpretable-by-construction systems.
evidence_acceptability: The proposal seeks compliance through technical design rather than evasion, privacy infringement or norm-violating workarounds.
evidence_implementability: Building formal log-emitting layers, benchmarking against standard architectures and validating Article 12 coverage requires major architecture research and engineering beyond routine logging integration.
evidence_applicability: The program directly targets automatic event recording and traceability required by Article 12 for high-risk systems, including Annex III use cases.
evidence_effectiveness: If realized, architectures that emit structured logs during the forward pass would provide the required traceability without sacrificing capability.

evidence_originality: Pioneering a tiered taxonomy validated against emerging guidance and published openly is uncommon among labs focused only on internal logging.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance ambiguity as a research question, turning logging obligations into publishable ML theory and standard-setting work.
evidence_acceptability: Openly publishing compliance-related research aligns with academic norms and does not conflict with legal or business expectations.
evidence_implementability: Developing sensitivity analyses and a taxonomy requires dedicated research staff time but uses existing ML literature and does not require new infrastructure.
evidence_applicability: The proposal targets the undefined substantial-modification boundary that governs when Article 12 logs must capture events.
evidence_effectiveness: It provides a decision rule for when Article 12(2)(a) logging triggers, reducing ambiguity in compliance without building the logging infrastructure itself.

evidence_originality: Conducting a compliance-readiness audit and reallocating R&D resources is a common, mundane management response expected from experienced labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal adds audit tools and project triage but still treats compliance as a logging practice to be managed around existing R&D rather than redefining the lab-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Portfolio audits and resource reprioritisation are normal governance practices that do not violate legal, social or business norms.
evidence_implementability: A structured audit using a standardised two-week rubric and quarterly board reporting requires only management time and coordination, not new technology.
evidence_applicability: The audit directly addresses the stated problem of deciding how to meet the logging mandate and adapt R&D resource allocation under scarce implementation budgets.
evidence_effectiveness: By identifying projects where retroactive logging is disproportionately costly, the audit enables selective compliance-by-design investment that contributes to meeting Article 12 without guaranteeing full logging coverage.

evidence_originality: A forkable internal SDK with unit tests for Article 12(3) biometric log fields is a common engineering reuse tactic expected from labs facing logging mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal keeps compliance as logging practice and only adds a reusable tooling element without changing the lab’s R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Building an internal logging SDK that records session timestamps, reference-database pointers, matched inputs and verifier identities complies with the AI Act and offends no norms.
evidence_implementability: Two engineers in one sprint extracting existing hooks into a parameterised SDK with retention config and publishing it to an internal registry is reasonably feasible with moderate effort.
evidence_applicability: The template directly addresses the stated problem by satisfying all four sub-requirements of Article 12(3) for Annex III point 1(a) high-risk biometric systems.
evidence_effectiveness: It will reliably produce compliant logs for future biometric projects, but it only covers Annex III 1(a) logging and does not solve the broader Article 12 mandate for all high-risk systems.

evidence_originality: Treating compliance logs as a first-of-its-kind multi-year drift dataset is unusual and shows imagination but is not presented as ingenious or surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal weaves mandatory logging into scientific research by using Article 12 logs as a longitudinal study instrument, changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Publishing anonymised aggregate drift findings from biometric systems is unusual but does not violate legal norms or sensibilities if properly anonymised.
evidence_implementability: Running a multi-year programme with quarterly log queries, post-doc analysis, and anonymised publication requires significant data-governance effort and cost for an R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: It addresses the stated problem of adapting R&D to the logging mandate by repurposing required logs for research value rather than merely implementing them.
evidence_effectiveness: The study assumes logs will already exist and does not guarantee implementation of Article 12 logging, so it only partially contributes to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: The dashboard uses standard observability tools like Kafka and Grafana to monitor log completeness, a common DevOps practice rather than an ingenious or surprising approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It adds new monitoring tools but keeps compliance as a logging practice without changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Internal log health monitoring is a routine engineering practice that violates no legal, social or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Standing up a per-pilot Kafka topic and Grafana panels requires modest engineering effort and infrastructure changes.
evidence_applicability: The dashboard directly targets the mandate to automatically record Article 12 events and enable traceability for post-market monitoring.
evidence_effectiveness: It will help ensure Article 12 events are captured in production but does not itself create the required logs or alter research, providing only partial assurance.

evidence_originality: The idea repurposes a CI/CD test harness as a regulatory compliance gate for AI Act logs, which is unusual and imaginative for an R&D lab.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves Article 12 logging obligations into the nightly prototyping cycle so compliance checking becomes part of R&D rather than a separate audit step.
evidence_acceptability: Building automated tests for required logs aligns with standard engineering norms and raises no legal or sensibility concerns.
evidence_implementability: It requires creating schema assertions and integrating them into existing nightly builds and issue tracker, a reasonably feasible engineering change.
evidence_applicability: The test suite directly targets the mandate to technically allow automatic recording of Article 12(2) event categories for high-risk systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would systematically catch missing log categories early and thereby solve the stated problem of meeting the logging mandate during R&D.

evidence_originality: Treating regulatory logging as a longitudinal natural experiment for drift and degradation is unusual and shows imagination beyond standard compliance.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces new research elements and changes the relationship between the lab’s R&D and its compliance obligations by weaving mandatory lifetime logs into the scientific agenda.
evidence_acceptability: Using mandated logs for internal research and peer-reviewed publication violates no legal, social or business norms and aligns with responsible AI transparency expectations.
evidence_implementability: Creating a dedicated post-deployment analytics team and a multi-year programme to mine operational logs requires staffing, data pipelines and governance changes beyond routine compliance.
evidence_applicability: The programme directly addresses the stated need to adapt R&D in response to Article 12 by repurposing the mandatory lifetime logging requirement as a research platform.
evidence_effectiveness: It contributes to adapting R&D to the mandate but does not itself implement or guarantee the automatic logging, traceability and record-keeping required by Articles 12(1)-(3).

evidence_originality: Reusing debugging/monitoring telemetry for regulatory logs and filing gap analyses is a common, mundane compliance tactic expected from AI R&D labs.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal treats compliance as a logging-practice upgrade using existing telemetry rather than changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Repurposing internal monitoring for compliance is a standard, legally unproblematic engineering practice that violates no norms.
evidence_implementability: It requires coordinated six-week gap analyses by project leads and platform-engineering patches to middleware, which is reasonably feasible but involves nontrivial cross-team changes.
evidence_applicability: Mapping existing telemetry to Article 12(2) and 12(3) requirements directly addresses how the lab meets the logging mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: Auditing current event streams and incrementally patching deltas into shared middleware can provide the Article 12(2)-(3) logs needed for traceability, post-market monitoring and risk identification.

evidence_originality: Making logging an architectural default in an internal SDK is an interesting engineering improvement but is a common, mundane approach to compliance automation.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal introduces new logging tools and processes but still treats Article 12 as a logging practice rather than changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding schema-driven logging in the shared prototyping SDK is a standard compliance engineering practice that violates no legal, social or political norms.
evidence_implementability: Extending an existing experiment-runner with async middleware and auto-wiring project templates requires some changes to core tooling but is reasonably feasible for an R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the stated problem of how to meet the Article 12 automatic record-keeping mandate for high-risk AI R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic timestamped event recording from first run will help meet Article 12(1) and traceability needs but does not by itself guarantee logging of all Article 12(2)-(3) specific risk-relevant events.

evidence_originality: Embedding compliance artifacts automatically at every pipeline stage is unusual for R&D labs and shows imaginative integration of regulatory evidence with scientific workflow.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The proposal weaves logging and documentation into each model iteration via a CI/CD hook, changing the relationship between research work and compliance rather than treating compliance as post-hoc.
evidence_acceptability: Integrating compliance into the research pipeline aligns with legal requirements and normative expectations for accountable AI development.
evidence_implementability: Building CI/CD hooks, metadata capture, and versioned documentation assembly requires cross-team engineering changes but is reasonably feasible with existing DevOps practices.
evidence_applicability: The proposal explicitly targets meeting Article 12 logging and documentation requirements for high-risk AI systems in the lab's R&D process.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic generation of Article 12 logs and technical documentation per iteration would directly satisfy the traceability and record-keeping mandate.

evidence_originality: Retrofitting structured event loggers into model pipelines is a common, mundane compliance engineering approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces a logging middleware tool and process but still treats compliance as standard logging practice without changing the lab’s R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Native automatic event logging for traceability is a common, legally required compliance practice that violates no norms or sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Embedding a lightweight logging middleware into existing training and inference frameworks with a two-person platform cell over two sprints is reasonably feasible using the current monitoring stack.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses how to meet Article 12’s automatic event-logging requirement for high-risk AI systems in the R&D lab.
evidence_effectiveness: The middleware natively records use-periods, reference databases queried, matched inputs and verifier identities as mandated by Article 12(1) and 12(3), solving the logging mandate.

evidence_originality: Automated diffing of model weights, schemas and lineage to trigger Act-specific logs is unusual among expected lab responses and shows imagination in operationalizing 'substantial modification'.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The gate embeds logging and substantial-modification assessment directly into the CI/CD workflow, weaving compliance into R&D rather than treating it as a separate audit task.
evidence_acceptability: A CI-based compliance gate is a standard engineering practice that does not violate legal, social or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a comparison service, similarity thresholds and sign-off holds requires non-trivial engineering changes to the CI runner and definition of legal criteria, so implementation is reasonably feasible but not trivial.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets Article 12(2)(a) traceability and automatic logging of events relevant to substantial modification, which is an identified part of the mandate.
evidence_effectiveness: It will reliably create the required event records for substantial modifications before deployment, but it does not address other Article 12 logging duties such as use-period recording or post-market monitoring logs.

evidence_originality: A drop-in decorator SDK with CI-gated import is a familiar engineering packaging of compliance logging rather than an ingenious or surprising approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: The idea introduces a new tooling element for logging but still treats compliance as logging practice and preserves the lab’s prototyping cadence and R&D workflow.
evidence_acceptability: Automatic recording of Article 12 event fields via an internal SDK is a standard compliance engineering practice that violates no legal, social or business norms.
evidence_implementability: The proposal is a lightweight Python-native middleware with a single decorator and pluggable backends plus CI enforcement, making logging a one-line change rather than a multi-day integration.
evidence_applicability: The SDK directly records timestamps, reference databases, matched inputs and verifier IDs to meet the Article 12 logging mandate for high-risk AI systems.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the event stream would provide the required automatic logs for traceability, post-market monitoring and risk situation identification from first commit.

evidence_originality: Operationalising Article 12(2)(a) as a public, challenge-driven anomalous-inference benchmark is unusual and shows imagination in the compliance domain.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves compliance-driven logging into the lab’s science by creating shared evaluation tools and external partnerships, changing the relationship between R&D and compliance obligations without breaking the research paradigm.
evidence_acceptability: Releasing an anonymised public benchmark and academic challenge for risk-event detection is a common research practice that violates no legal, social or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Curating synthetic and anonymised log sequences, defining standard detection metrics and hosting an annual community challenge requires data engineering, legal review and ongoing infrastructure, which is reasonably feasible but not low cost.
evidence_applicability: The proposal addresses an implied need for better anomaly-inference methods to satisfy Article 12(2)(a), rather than directly providing the required automatic event logging for the lab’s products.
evidence_effectiveness: The benchmark advances external methods for identifying risk situations from logs but does not install logging capabilities in the lab’s own high-risk AI systems, so it only partially helps meet the Article 12 mandate.

evidence_originality: Shift-left automated testing for regulatory logs is a familiar DevOps pattern applied to AI compliance, making it interesting but not surprising.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces automated schema validators into the CI pipeline but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing the lab's R&D-compliance relationship.
evidence_acceptability: Embedding compliance checks in CI is a standard norm-conforming practice that does not violate legal or business sensibilities.
evidence_implementability: Adding a validation stage to an existing CI pipeline requires building schemas and validators, which is reasonably feasible with some engineering effort.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly addresses the lab's need to meet Article 12 automatic logging and traceability mandates by validating logs in development.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the CI gates would ensure every prototype emits Article 12-compliant logs before integration, solving the core compliance verification problem.

evidence_originality: A reusable logging middleware SDK for AI prototypes is a familiar engineering pattern rather than an ingenious surprise.

evidence_acceptability: Automated logging for regulatory compliance aligns with legal obligations and normal engineering practice.
evidence_implementability: Building a shared SDK and pipeline hooks requires moderate engineering effort but is feasible within an existing lab.
evidence_applicability: The scaffold directly addresses how to meet Article 12 logging requirements in R&D.
evidence_effectiveness: Automatic capture of timestamps, input references and outputs by default provides the traceability logs Article 12 mandates across prototypes.

evidence_originality: Centralized versioned documentation with automated staleness alerts tied to CI/CD is a common, mundane compliance engineering approach.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It weaves logging and documentation updates into the R&D workflow via CI/CD triggers, changing how compliance relates to model development.
evidence_acceptability: The proposal uses standard document control and log retention practices that comply with Article 12 and Recital 71 without violating legal or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Building a versioned repository with CI/CD hooks requires engineering work and process changes but is reasonably feasible for an AI R&D lab.
evidence_applicability: It directly addresses the mandate to keep records current and automatically log events throughout a high-risk system's lifetime as required by Article 12 and Recital 71.
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented, the registry would provide continuous, auditable documentation and logs that satisfy traceability, post-market monitoring, and regulatory review requirements.

evidence_originality: Repurposing existing telemetry for compliance logging is a common, mundane industry approach to regulatory mandates.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It introduces reusable logging middleware and schema modules but still treats compliance as a logging practice rather than changing the lab’s R&D-compliance relationship.

evidence_effectiveness: A reusable middleware mapping Article 12(2)(a)–(c) event categories would provide automatic lifetime logs and reduce per-project overhead, contributing substantially to meeting the mandate.

evidence_originality: Building a shared cross-project log observatory for long-term drift and causal inference is unusual and imaginatively reuses compliance data.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logs from a cost center into a core scientific instrument, changing how R&D relates to regulatory obligations and what the lab researches.
evidence_acceptability: Internal use of already-required logs for performance monitoring and research complies with the AI Act and raises no normative concerns.
evidence_implementability: Normalizing schemas across projects and running longitudinal anomaly detection requires non-trivial engineering but is reasonably feasible within an existing infrastructure plan.
evidence_applicability: It directly applies mandated logs to adapt R&D by building a longitudinal drift research program required by the compliance context.

evidence_originality: The dashboard concept is familiar in regulated labs and its framing as funding narrative support shows only modest imagination.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: It reframes compliance logging from a cost burden into an operational research capability and funding asset, changing how R&D relates to compliance obligations.
evidence_acceptability: A read-only monitoring dashboard that uses legally required logs does not violate legal, social or business norms.
evidence_implementability: Using an existing visualisation stack with one postdoc for a read-only panel is reasonably feasible but requires dedicated staff time and threshold calibration.
evidence_applicability: The proposal builds on Article 12 event logs mandated for high-risk systems to provide the traceability and post-market monitoring required by Articles 72 and 26(5).
evidence_effectiveness: If implemented it would turn mandatory logs into actionable early warnings, contributing to adaptation to the mandate but not itself creating the required logging capability.

evidence_originality: Using a customer-funded pilot to build an IP-retained, reusable logging architecture is unusual compared with typical internal one-off compliance implementations.
evidence_paradigm_relatedness: Turning compliance logging into a reusable IP asset and a customer-funded offering changes the lab's R&D-compliance relationship beyond one-off logging practice.

evidence_acceptability: Privacy-preserving logging aligns with data protection norms and regulatory expectations, so it is socially and legally acceptable.
evidence_implementability: Building a prototype middleware with differential privacy or homomorphic encryption and benchmarking across multiple model families requires substantial engineering and research effort beyond routine logging deployment.
evidence_applicability: The proposal directly targets Article 12's automatic logging and traceability requirements for high-risk AI systems.
evidence_effectiveness: Even if technically feasible, privacy-preserving logs may reduce the identifiability required for Article 12 traceability and post-market monitoring, so it helps but does not guarantee full compliance.

evidence_originality: Centralized, project-agnostic logging middleware inherited at scaffold time is a common, mundane engineering solution for regulatory record-keeping.

evidence_applicability: It targets the lab’s decision of how to meet the Article 12 logging mandate by making logging a default inherited dependency for all high-risk projects.
evidence_effectiveness: The middleware automatically embeds timestamp, provenance and operational event capture in every high-risk prototype runtime, directly providing the Article 12(1) technical logging capability required for traceability and post-market monitoring.

evidence_originality: Framing mandatory auditability as an empirical cost-of-transparency research program is unusual and shows imagination beyond standard compliance engineering.

evidence_applicability: The study addresses the implied problem of how compliance costs affect R&D choices rather than directly delivering mandated logs.
evidence_effectiveness: Measuring performance loss from logging informs adaptation decisions but does not itself implement the required traceability systems.
